headline: High-risk shared-filesystem and broad-egress pair: Goose can read/write the workspace while the other agent can emit untrusted content and both can exfiltrate via network.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can produce content-writing outputs, and B reads/writes the filesystem plus uses MCP and shell tools. Because B's shared_state_with_other_instances is via filesystem, A's output can reach B through files and be treated as instructions. This is not proven as a default parser hijack, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF agent_a output is written into a file that agent_b reads as task input, injection becomes active.
IF agent_b parses file contents as instructions without provenance checks, attacker-controlled text can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate A and B into different directories.
Add a provenance header to every file passed from A to B.
Require B to ignore imperative text inside A outputs.
Use a manual review step before B executes any file-derived instruction.

B_data_leakage.rationale: B touches source code and files in cwd, and its shared state is via filesystem; A has broad network egress. If sensitive files are placed in the shared workspace, A can potentially transmit them outward. The profiles do not show PHI or a guaranteed leak path, so medium fits the default shared-workspace risk.
conditions: IF sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, agent_a can access them indirectly through shared files.
IF agent_a is instructed to summarize or upload workspace contents, exfiltration becomes possible.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared cwd.
Mount separate workspaces for each agent.
Disable network egress for A during shared-file handling.
Scan shared files for secrets before either agent runs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: B has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and supports multiple instances with shared_state via filesystem. A is a content-writing agent that can also reach the network. Concurrent edits to the same workspace or git state can overwrite each other, and the lack of locking makes the default pair dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent commits or file writes can conflict.
IF the orchestrator does not provide file locks, last-writer-wins corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate branches or worktrees.
Serialize write access with a lock file.
Disable git mutation for one agent.
Run one agent read-only until the other finishes.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces content that B can ingest from files or MCP-driven workflows, and B has shell and filesystem authority. That creates a default path where B may act on A's unverified output. The profiles do not show fully autonomous downstream actions, so medium is the highest supported severity.
conditions: IF B uses A's output as task input without verification, errors cascade into actions.
IF A's output contains incorrect commands or facts, B can execute them via shell or file edits.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against source files.
Add a second-pass review before shell execution.
Restrict A to drafting only, not command generation.
Log and diff all A-to-B handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for A, while B handles model provider keys and extension tokens and runs on-machine. The pairwise compliance risk is therefore limited to general policy gaps rather than a documented breach path, and A is not cited for a distinct compliance regime.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into the shared workspace, local handling policies must be checked.
IF an extension sends retained data to a third-party provider, compliance review is required.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair.
Review provider and extension retention settings.
Disable unnecessary extensions.
Document the data flow before deployment.
